subject: Physics
title: Electricity - Complete Learning Module
outcomes: Define electric current and potential difference with their SI units
Calculate resistance from length, area, and resistivity
Analyse series and parallel combinations of resistors
Apply the heating effect of current and electric power formulae
Calculate electrical energy consumption in kWh and its cost
Solve board-style numericals on circuits, power, and energy

concepts.title: Electric Current and Potential Difference
concepts.explanation: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, given by I = Q/t. Its SI unit is the ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 coulomb per second. Conventional current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a cell, while electrons drift in the opposite direction. Potential difference between two points is the work done to move a unit charge from one point to the other, V = W/Q, and its SI unit is the volt (V).
key_points: Current I = Q/t; SI unit ampere (A).
Conventional current is opposite to the direction of electron flow.
Potential difference V = W/Q; SI unit volt (V).
An ammeter measures current and is connected in series; a voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel.
concepts.real_life_example: A torch bulb glows because a cell maintains a potential difference that drives current through the filament.

concepts.title: Ohm's Law and Resistance
concepts.explanation: Ohm's law states that the current through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature remains constant. This gives V = IR, where R is the resistance of the conductor. Resistance is the opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of current, and its SI unit is the ohm. A resistor with a straight-line V-I graph through the origin obeys Ohm's law and is called an ohmic conductor.
key_points: Ohm's law: V = IR at constant temperature.
SI unit of resistance is the ohm.
The V-I graph of an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin.
Resistance depends on the material, length, area of cross-section, and temperature of the conductor.
concepts.real_life_example: A filament bulb and a heater coil are made of materials chosen for their resistance so that they convert electrical energy into light and heat.

concepts.title: Factors Affecting Resistance and Resistivity
concepts.explanation: The resistance of a uniform conductor is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its area of cross-section. It also depends on the nature of the material and its temperature. These facts combine into R = rho L / A, where rho is the resistivity of the material. Resistivity is a property of the material itself and its SI unit is the ohm metre; metals have low resistivity while insulators have very high resistivity.
key_points: R is directly proportional to length L.
R is inversely proportional to area of cross-section A.
R = rho L / A, where rho is resistivity.
Resistivity is a material property measured in ohm metre; it changes with temperature.
concepts.real_life_example: House wiring uses thick copper wires of low resistivity so that they carry current without overheating, while the thin filament of a bulb has high resistance and glows.

concepts.title: Resistors in Series and Parallel
concepts.explanation: When resistors are joined in series, the same current flows through each of them and the total potential difference is the sum of the individual potential differences. The equivalent resistance is Req = R1 + R2 + R3 + ..., which is greater than the largest individual resistance. When resistors are joined in parallel, the potential difference across each is the same and the total current is the sum of the branch currents. The equivalent resistance is given by 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 + ..., which is less than the smallest individual resistance.
key_points: Series: same current, voltages add, Req = R1 + R2 + ...
Parallel: same voltage, currents add, 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...
Series equivalent resistance is larger than the largest resistor.
Parallel equivalent resistance is smaller than the smallest resistor.
concepts.real_life_example: Domestic appliances are connected in parallel so that each receives the full supply voltage and can be switched on or off independently.

concepts.title: Heating Effect of Current and Electric Power
concepts.explanation: When current flows through a resistor, electrical energy is converted into heat because the resistor opposes the flow of charge. The heat produced is H = I^2 R t, which is Joule's law of heating. Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed, P = VI = I^2 R = V^2 / R. The SI unit of power is the watt (W), and 1 W = 1 joule per second.
key_points: Joule's law of heating: H = I^2 R t.
Electric power: P = VI = I^2 R = V^2 / R.
SI unit of power is the watt (W).
The heating effect is useful in heaters, irons, and fuses but is an energy loss in transmission wires.
concepts.real_life_example: An electric iron, geyser, and toaster work on the heating effect of current, while a fuse melts and breaks the circuit when current becomes too large.

concepts.title: Commercial Unit of Electrical Energy and Household Circuits
concepts.explanation: Electrical energy is the product of power and time, E = P x t. For large amounts of energy, the commercial unit is the kilowatt-hour (kWh), where 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J. One kilowatt-hour is the energy consumed by a 1 kW appliance used for 1 hour, and it is commonly called one unit of electricity. In household wiring, appliances are connected in parallel and each circuit is protected by a fuse or miniature circuit breaker (MCB).
key_points: Electrical energy E = P x t.
1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J = one commercial unit.
The electricity meter records energy in kWh.
Household appliances are connected in parallel and protected by fuses or MCBs.
concepts.real_life_example: An electricity bill lists the number of units consumed; a 100 W bulb used for 10 hours consumes 1 kWh, which is one unit.

worked_examples.title: Electric current from charge and time
worked_examples.problem: A charge of 60 C flows through a conductor in 1 minute. Find the current.
solution: Step 2: Convert time to seconds: t = 1 minute = 60 s.
Step 4: The current through the conductor is 1 ampere.
worked_examples.board_tip: Always convert time to seconds before substituting into I = Q/t.
worked_examples.exam_tip: 1 ampere means 1 coulomb of charge passes a point in 1 second.

worked_examples.title: Ohm's law: current through a resistor
worked_examples.problem: A potential difference of 6 V is applied across a resistor of resistance 3 ohm. Find the current through the resistor.
solution: Step 1: Use Ohm's law V = IR.
Step 3: Substitute V = 6 V and R = 3 ohm.
worked_examples.board_tip: Keep V in volts and R in ohms so that the current comes out in amperes.
worked_examples.exam_tip: If V doubles at constant resistance, the current also doubles.

worked_examples.title: Resistance from resistivity, length, and area
worked_examples.problem: A copper wire of length 2 m and area of cross-section 1 x 10^-6 m^2 has resistivity 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre. Find its resistance.
solution: Step 1: Use R = rho L / A.
Step 2: Substitute rho = 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm m, L = 2 m, and A = 1 x 10^-6 m^2.
worked_examples.board_tip: Watch the powers of ten when dividing numbers in scientific notation.
worked_examples.exam_tip: A longer or thinner wire has more resistance; a thicker wire has less.

worked_examples.title: Series and parallel equivalent resistance
worked_examples.problem: Two resistors of 6 ohm and 3 ohm are connected first in series and then in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance in each case.
solution: Step 1: In series, Req = R1 + R2 = 6 + 3 = 9 ohm.
Step 5: The series value is larger than either resistor, while the parallel value is smaller than either.
worked_examples.board_tip: For two resistors in parallel, Req = (R1 x R2)/(R1 + R2) is a quick check.
worked_examples.exam_tip: The parallel equivalent is always less than the smallest resistance in the combination.

worked_examples.title: Power and energy of a bulb
worked_examples.problem: An electric bulb is rated 220 V, 100 W. Find the current through it, its resistance, and the energy consumed in 5 hours.
solution: Step 1: Use P = VI, so I = P/V = 100/220 = 0.4545 A.
Step 3: Energy E = P x t with P = 100 W = 0.1 kW and t = 5 h.
Step 5: In joules, E = 0.5 x 3.6 x 10^6 = 1.8 x 10^6 J.
worked_examples.answer: I = 0.45 A; R = 484 ohm; energy = 0.5 kWh = 1.8 x 10^6 J.
worked_examples.board_tip: Use kW with hours to get energy directly in kWh.
worked_examples.exam_tip: The rated power is consumed only when the bulb is operated at its rated voltage.

problems.question: A 6 ohm resistor is connected in series with a parallel combination of 6 ohm and 3 ohm resistors. The combination is connected across a 16 V battery. Find the total current, the voltage across the parallel combination, and the current in each parallel branch.
solution: Step 1: Parallel part: 1/Rp = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6, so Rp = 2 ohm.
Step 3: Total current I = V/Req = 16/8 = 2 A.
Step 4: Voltage across the parallel part = I x Rp = 2 x 2 = 4 V.
Step 5: Current through 6 ohm branch = 4/6 = 0.667 A.
Step 6: Current through 3 ohm branch = 4/3 = 1.333 A.
problems.final_answer: I = 2 A; parallel voltage = 4 V; branch currents = 0.667 A and 1.333 A.

complex.question: A 100 W bulb and a 60 W bulb, both rated 220 V, are connected in series across 220 V. Which glows brighter?
options: The 60 W bulb, because it has higher resistance
The 100 W bulb, because it is rated higher

explanation.correct: In series the current is the same, and P = I^2 R; the 60 W bulb has the higher resistance, so it dissipates more power.

wrong_options.1: The rating applies at 220 V individually, not in this series circuit.
wrong_options.2: Their resistances differ, so they do not glow equally.
wrong_options.3: Both will glow, though below their rated brightness.

complex.question: A 100 W bulb and a 60 W bulb, both rated 220 V, are connected in parallel across 220 V. Which glows brighter?
options: The 100 W bulb, because it has lower resistance
The 60 W bulb, because it has higher resistance

explanation.correct: In parallel each gets 220 V, so the 100 W bulb consumes more power and glows brighter.

wrong_options.1: Higher resistance at the same voltage means lower power.
wrong_options.2: The rated powers differ, so the brightness differs.
wrong_options.3: Both receive the full 220 V and glow.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Current is used up as it flows around a circuit.
common_misconceptions.correction: Charge is conserved; the current is the same at every point in a series circuit, while electrical energy is converted into other forms.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Electrons flow from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.
common_misconceptions.correction: Conventional current flows from positive to negative, but electrons drift from negative to positive.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Resistance depends only on the length of a wire.
common_misconceptions.correction: Resistance also depends on the area of cross-section, the material, and the temperature.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A thicker wire has more resistance.
common_misconceptions.correction: A thicker wire has a larger area of cross-section and therefore less resistance, since R is inversely proportional to A.

common_misconceptions.misconception: An ammeter is connected in parallel with a component.
common_misconceptions.correction: An ammeter is connected in series so that the current to be measured passes through it.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A voltmeter is connected in series with a component.
common_misconceptions.correction: A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component whose potential difference is to be measured.

common_misconceptions.misconception: One kilowatt-hour is a unit of power.
common_misconceptions.correction: One kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, equal to 3.6 x 10^6 J; the watt is the unit of power.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Electric power and electrical energy mean the same thing.
common_misconceptions.correction: Power is the rate of energy consumption, P = E/t; energy is power multiplied by time.
